questions.question: Which Five-Year Plan primarily focused on the 'Garibi Hatao' initiative?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Fifth Five-Year Plan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Fifth Five Year Plan: Its duration was 1974 to 1978. This plan focussed on Garibi Hatao, employment, justice, agricultural production, and defense.
 
• The Electricity Supply Act was amended in 1975, a Twenty-point program was launched in 1975, the Minimum Needs Programme (MNP), and the Indian National Highway System was introduced. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• First Five Year Plan: It was launched for the duration of 1951 to 1956, under the leadership of Jawaharlal Nehru. It was based on the Harrod-Domar model with a few modifications. Its main focus was on the agricultural development of the country.
 
• Second Five Year Plan: It was made for the duration of 1956 to 1961, under the leadership of Jawaharlal Nehru. It was based on the P.C. Mahalanobis Model made in the year 1953. Its main focus was on the industrial development of the country.
 
• Third Five-Year Plan: It was made for the duration of 1961 to 1966, under the leadership of Jawaharlal Nehru. This plan is also called ‘Gadgil Yojna’, after the Deputy Chairman of Planning Commission D.R. Gadgil. The main target of this plan was to make the economy independent. The stress was laid on agriculture and the improvement in the production of wheat. 
 
• Plan Holidays: Due to the failure of the previous plan, the government announced three annual plans called Plan Holidays from 1966 to 1969. The main reason behind the plan holidays was the Indo-Pakistani war and the Sino-India war, leading to the failure of the third Five Year Plan.
 
• Fourth Five-Year Plan: Its duration was from 1969 to 1974, under the leadership of Indira Gandhi. There were two main objectives of this plan i.e. growth with stability and progressive achievement of self-reliance.
 
• Rolling Plan: After the termination of the fifth Five Year Plan, the Rolling Plan came into effect from 1978 to 1980. In 1980, Congress rejected the Rolling Plan, and a new sixth Five Year Plan was introduced. 
 
• Sixth Five Year Plan: Its duration was from 1980 to 1985, under the leadership of Indira Gandhi. The basic objective of this plan was economic liberalization by eradicating poverty and achieving technological self-reliance.
 
• Seventh Five Year Plan: Its duration was from 1985 to 1990, under the leadership of Rajiv Gandhi. The objectives of this plan include the establishment of a self-sufficient economy, opportunities for productive employment, and up-gradation of technology.
 
• Eighth Five Year Plan: Its duration was from 1992 to 1997, under the leadership of P.V. Narasimha Rao. In this plan, the top priority was given to the development of human resources i.e. employment, education, and public health.
 
• Ninth Five Year Plan: Its duration was from 1997 to 2002, under the leadership of Atal Bihari Vajpayee. The main focus of this plan was “Growth with Social Justice and Equality”.
 
• Tenth Five Year Plan: Its duration was from 2002 to 2007, under the leadership of Atal Bihari Vajpayee and Manmohan Singh. II. This plan aimed to double the Per Capita Income of India in the next 10 years.
 
• Eleventh Five Year Plan: Its duration was from 2007 to 2012, under the leadership of Manmohan Singh. It was prepared by C. Rangarajan.Its main theme was “rapid and more inclusive growth”. Twelfth Five Year Plan: Its duration is from 2012 to 2017, under the leadership of Manmohan Singh. Its main theme is “Faster, More Inclusive and Sustainable Growth”.

questions.question: In which musical note did Newland put the metals Co and Ni with halogens?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Do**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• John Newlands, a British chemist, proposed the **Law of Octaves in 1864**.
 
• This law stated that when elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic mass, every eighth element has properties similar to the first.
 
• He compared this pattern to the octaves of music, where every eighth note is similar to the first.
 
• However, **Newlands' Law of Octaves **had limitations.
 
• It didn't work for all elements, especially those with higher atomic masses.
 
• To accommodate all the known elements, he had to place two elements in the same slot in some cases.
 
• One such instance was with cobalt (**Co**) and nickel (**Ni**), which he placed in the same slot as the halogens.
 
• This placement highlights the limitations of Newland's classification system.
 
• While it was a significant step towards understanding the periodic relationships between elements, it was not entirely accurate and was eventually superseded by more comprehensive periodic tables, such as **Mendeleev's Periodic Table**.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT correct with regards to the history of calculating National Income (NI) in India?

options.text: First attempt to compute NI was made by Dadabhai Naoroji.
First official attempt to compute NI was made by PC Mahalanobis.
Dadabhai Naoroji divided the Indian economy into two parts: primary sector and secondary sector.
First scientific method to compute NI was used by Dr VKRV Rao.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Dadabhai Naoroji divided the Indian economy into two parts: primary sector and secondary sector**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• National income is the total income of all the residents of the country.
 
• Thus, it is the total income of the country.
 
• It is considered to be one of the most important attributes for comparing the development of countries.
 
• The National Income formula equals GDP + Foreign Production by National Residents – Domestic Production by Non-National Residents.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Dadabhai Naoroji**

 
• Dadabhai Naoroji, known as the Grand Old Man of India, was a leading figure in the early Indian independence movement and a founder of the Indian National Congress.
 
 
• His activities were mainly in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
 
• The Indian Independence League, however, was primarily active during the 1940s, significantly after Naoroji's most impactful years and following his death in 1917.
 
• This organization sought to obtain independence for India from British rule during World War II, with notable connections to Subhas Chandra Bose and the Indian National Army (INA).
 
• Naoroji founded or was associated with several organizations, like the Bombay Association (the oldest political organization in Bombay), the East India Association (established in London to discuss Indian affairs), and Gyan Prasarak Mandali (for the education of adult men in Bombay).
 
• These affiliations reflected his focus on political advocacy, economic theories (notably the Drain Theory), and social reform both in India and the UK.
 
• The Indian Independence League's context and methods, focused on leveraging the geopolitical situations during World War II for India's independence through more direct action, were distinct and not within Naoroji's lifetime or direct activities.
 
 
 
• **​PC Mahalanobis**
 
 
• The Second five-year plan was based on the Mahalanobis model, an economic development model developed by the Indian statistician Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis in 1953.
 
• PC Mahalanobis established the Indian Statistical Institute (ISI) in Calcutta in 1931 and for the same reason, he is known as the father of Indian Statistics. He was a member of the first Planning Commission of free India.
 
• The second five-year plan was for the year 1956-1961.
 
• The second five-year plan focused on the development of the public sector and rapid Industrialisation. The plan attempted to determine a balanced allocation of investment between productive sectors in order to maximize long-run economic growth. 
 
• As a result, hydroelectric power projects across the country and five steel plants at Bhilai, Durgapur, and Rourkela were established with the help of Russia, Britain (the U.K), and West Germany respectively. Coal production was increased. More railway lines were added all over the country.
 
• The Tata Institute of Fundamental Research and Atomic Energy Commission of India was established to promote research in India.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT about the Directive Principles of State Policy?

options.text: They promote welfare of individuals. Hence, they are personal and individualistic.
These have moral and political sanctions.
They aim at establishing social and economic democracy in the country.
They are positive, as they require the State to do certain things.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**They promote welfare of individuals. Hence, they are personal and individualistic**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The Directive Principles of State Policy of India are the guidelines or principles given to the institutes for governing India and are provided in Part IV of the Constitution of India.
 
• Directive Principles of State Policy aim to create social and economic conditions under which the citizens can lead a good life.
 
• They also aim to establish social and economic democracy through a welfare state. Directive principles are classified under the following categories; economic, socialistic, political, executive, justice and legal, administrative, environmental, protection of monuments, peace, and security.

Hence, it can be said that the Directive Principles of State Policy are fundamental for the Governance of the state.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Features of DPSPs

 
 
• The phrase ‘Directive Principles of State Policy’ denotes the ideals that the State should keep in mind while formulating policies and enacting laws.
 
• These are the constitutional instructions or recommendations to the State in legislative, executive, and administrative matters. According to Article 36, the term ‘State’ in Part IV has the same meaning as in Part III dealing with Fundamental Rights.
 
• Therefore, it includes the legislative and executive organs of the central and state governments, all local authorities, and all other public authorities in the country.
 
• The Directive Principles resemble the ‘Instrument of Instructions’ enumerated in the Government of India Act of 1935.
 
• In the words of Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, ‘the Directive Principles are like the instrument of instructions, which were issued to the Governor-General and to the Governors of the colonies of India by the British Government under the Government of India Act of 1935. What is called Directive Principles is merely another name for the instrument of instruction. The only difference is that they are instructions to the legislature and the executive’.
 
• The Directive Principles constitute a very comprehensive economic, social and political program for a modern democratic State.
 
• They aim at realizing the high ideals of justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity as outlined in the Preamble to the Constitution.
 
• They embody the concept of a ‘welfare state’ and not that of a ‘police state’, which existed during the colonial era3. In brief, they seek to establish economic and social democracy in the country.
 
• The Directive Principles are non-justiciable in nature, that is, they are not legally enforceable by the courts for their violation.
 
• Therefore, the government (Central, state, and local) cannot be compelled to implement them.
 
• Nevertheless, the Constitution (Article 37) itself says that these principles are fundamental in the governance of the country and it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws.
 
• The Directive Principles, though nonjusticiable in nature, help the courts in examining and determining the constitutional validity of a law.
 
• The Supreme Court has ruled many times that in determining the constitutionality of any law if a court finds that the law in question seeks to give effect to a Directive Principle, it may consider such law to be ‘reasonable’ in relation to Article 14 (equality before law) or Article 19 (six freedoms) and thus save such law from unconstitutionality.

questions.question: The Parliament passed the Marine Aids to Navigation Bill, 2021 to repeal and replace which of the following Acts?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The Lighthouse Act,1927**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Marine Aids to Navigation Bill, 2021 repealed and replaced the Lighthouse Act of 1927.**
 
• Lighthouse Act of 1927
 
 
• **This act regulated lighthouses and navigational techniques in India for almost nine decades.**
 
 
 
• Marine Aids to Navigation Bill, 2021
 
 
• This **bill was introduced in Lok Sabha on March 15, 2021.**
 
• I**t aims to**: 
 
 
• Provide a framework for the development, maintenance, and management of aids to navigation in India 
 
• Improve the legal framework for matters related to aids to navigation and vessel traffic services 
 
• Manage vessel traffic services to enhance the safety and efficiency of shipping 
 
• Develop lighthouses for education, culture, and tourism 
 
 
 
 
 
• T**he Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways adopted this initiative to repeal colonial laws and replace them** with legislation that caters to the modern needs of the maritime industry. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **The Dangerous Machines (Regulation) Act, 1983**

 
 
• This act was enacted to regulate the manufacture, import, and use of dangerous machines and to ensure safety measures to protect workers from injuries while operating such machinery.
 
• It mandates the registration of dangerous machines, along with guidelines for their operation, maintenance, and safety protocols to prevent accidents and injuries.
 
 
 
• **The Personal Injuries (Emergency Provisions) Act, 1962**
 
 
• This act was introduced to provide immediate relief and compensation to individuals who suffer personal injuries during emergencies, such as natural disasters or accidents.
 
• It establishes a framework for assessing and compensating victims, ensuring timely financial support for medical expenses and rehabilitation.
 
 
 
• **The Dourine Act, 1910**
 
 
• This act was enacted to control and prevent the spread of dourine, a venereal disease affecting horses, which could have significant implications for equine health and the livestock industry.
 
• It includes provisions for the examination, isolation, and treatment of infected animals, as well as guidelines for the disposal of affected livestock to prevent the disease's transmission.

questions.question: Mahabalipuram emerged as an important centre of temple architecture under which of the following kingdoms of south India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pallava**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Pallava**

 
 
• Simhavishnu was the founder of the Pallava dynasty.
 
• The Pallava dynasty was a Tamil dynasty that ruled parts of South India from the 3rd century to the 9th century.
 
• Simhavishnu's reign marked the rise of the Pallavas to prominence in the region.
 
• The Pallavas are known for their patronage of architecture, particularly the rock-cut temples of Mahabalipuram.
 
• The dynasty played a crucial role in the cultural and political history of South India.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Chola**

 
 
• Vijayalaya Chola (reigned 848–871 CE) is widely regarded as the founder of the Chola dynasty that ruled over a significant portion of the Indian subcontinent from the 9th to the 13th centuries.
 
• Before Vijayalaya, the Cholas were a minor dynasty ruling from Uraiyur (modern-day Tiruchirappalli).
 
• Vijayalaya established the Chola capital at Thanjavur (modern-day Tanjore) after defeating the Muttaraiyar chieftain and establishing Chola supremacy in the region.
 
• He is credited with reviving the Chola power and laying the foundation for the future expansion of the Chola empire under his successors.
 
 
 
• **Chera **
 
 
• The Chera kingdom of Mahodayapuram was established in the ninth century in the south-western part of the peninsula, part of the present-day Kerala.
 
• The Chera kingdom played a pivotal role in the history of South India.
 
• The region's significant historical and cultural contributions include the introduction of Malayalam, which became prominent in inscriptions during this period.
 
• The association of the Chera kingdom with the South-Western part of the Indian peninsula highlights the geocultural significance of Kerala in Indian history, especially in relation to the development of regional languages and script.
 
• Moreover, the geographical location of the Chera kingdom contributed to its maritime commerce and cultural exchanges with distant lands, enhancing the spread of its cultural and linguistic influence.
 
 

 
• Chalukya dynasty

 
 
• They ruled in southern India from the 6th century.
 
• There were three types of Chalukyas,
 
 
• Badami Chalukyas
 
• Eastern Chalukyas
 
• Western Chalukyas
 
 
 
• Their capital was Badami.
 
• They followed Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism as well.
 
• They had a monarchial structure with King as its head.
 
• The chief queen was known as Tattamahish.
 
• King had all the judicial as well as administrative powers

questions.question: The Indian Constitution has established ________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**independent judicial system**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The Government of India Act, 1935 was a British law that established a federal system of government in India.

 
 
• It was the most important source of inspiration for the framers of the Indian Constitution.
 
• The Act provided for a bicameral legislature, a federal court, and a system of provincial autonomy.
 
• It also guaranteed fundamental rights to the people of India.
 
 
 
• The other options are incorrect.

 
• The Constitution of Britain is a unitary system of government, while the Constitution of Ireland is a republic.
 
• The Indian Council Act, 1919 was a less comprehensive document than the Government of India Act, 1935.
 
• The Government of India Act, 1935 was not without its flaws.
 
 
• However, it was a significant step forward in the development of self-government in India.
 
• It provided the basis for the Indian Constitution, which is one of the most progressive constitutions in the world.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

Here are some of the specific provisions of the Government of India Act, 1935 that were incorporated into the Indian Constitution:

 
• The federal system of government
 
• The bicameral legislature
 
• The federal court
 
• The system of provincial autonomy
 
• The guarantee of fundamental rights

The Indian Constitution also incorporated some provisions from other sources, such as the American Constitution, the Irish Constitution, and the British Magna Carta. However, the Government of India Act, 1935 was the most important source of inspiration for the framers of the Indian Constitution.

questions.question: Which organisms are classified as Aves?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Birds**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Aves is a class of vertebrates that comprises the birds' species.
 
• Birds are egg-laying animals, have fur, two legs, and are endothermic.
 
• They are found worldwide, and their size ranges from 5 cm (bee hummingbird) to 2.75 m (ostrich).
 
• Ostrich is the organism that belongs to the Aves as they have those characteristics that are found in the members of the class Aves.
 
• The ostrich is typical of a group of flightless birds called ratites. 
 
• There are two living species of ostrich: the common ostrich (*Struthio camelus*) and the Somali ostrich (*Struthio molybdophanes*).​

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Aves:

 
 
• The class Aves includes birds or flying vertebrates.
 
• A characteristic feature of Aves is the presence of feathers.
 
• The birds are unique in having a coat of feathers and in resting on the hindlimbs alone.
 
• Respiration takes place only by the lungs.
 
• Lungs are respiratory organs, which are spongy, inelastic, and are connected to large air sacs.
 
• Endoskeleton is bony, but delicate and light.
 
• Bones are pneumatic i.e., contain air cavities to reduce weight.
 
• These are warm-blooded animals.
 
• Example - *Covus* (Crow), *Neophron *(Vulture)
